segments.text: ఆరవ (ārava) — "sixth".
ఆరు becomes ఆరవ (ārava), and this is the shortest ordinal in the ten: three syllables, two of them the number itself.
ఆరవ రోజు (ārava rōju) — the sixth day.

The numbers six to ten were the ones the first numbers lesson called Telugu's wandering half, the place where it drifts furthest from Tamil and Kannada. The ordinal ending does not care. Whatever shape the cardinal arrived in, -వ goes on it.

segments.source: [PAUSE 1s]

segments.instruction: ārava

segments.instruction: the swap — āru becomes ārava
segments.source: [YOU SAY: the swap — *āru* → *ārava*]

segments.instruction: ārava rōju — the sixth day
segments.source: [YOU SAY: *ārava rōju* — the sixth day]
[PAUSE 3s]

segments.text: Say the sixth. (ఆరవ (ārava).) What was traded for the ending? (The final u of ఆరు.) And does the ending change for the wandering half of the numbers? (No — it is the same -వ.)

segments.text: ఏడవ (ēḍava) — "seventh".
ఏడు becomes ఏడవ (ēḍava). Hold the ē long — the letter ఏ is the long one, and its short partner ఎ is a different letter and a different word.
ఏడవ వారం (ēḍava vāraṁ) — the seventh week.

Seven weeks is a useful thing to be able to say and a good place to hear that the ordinal is doing work no cardinal can do: ఏడు వారం would be seven weeks, a quantity. ఏడవ (ēḍava) వారం is the seventh one, a position.

segments.text: Say the seventh. (ఏడవ (ēḍava).) Which vowel opens it, the long or the short one? (The long ఏ.) And what is the difference between ఏడు వారం and ఏడవ (ēḍava) వారం? (Seven weeks against the seventh week.)

segments.text: ఎనిమిదవ (enimidava) — "eighth".

ఎనిమిది becomes ఎనిమిదవ (enimidava), and here the vowel that goes is an i, not a u. Every ordinal so far has traded a final u; this one and the next trade a final i, because that is what their cardinals happen to end in.
Which is the useful way to hold the rule: it is not "drop the u", it is drop whatever vowel is at the end. The ending does not know which vowel it replaced.
Note the short ఎ at the front, against the long ఏ of the last lesson.

segments.instruction: short ఎ here, long ఏ in ēḍava
segments.source: [YOU SAY: short *ఎ* here, long *ఏ* in *ēḍava*]
[PAUSE 3s]

segments.text: Say the eighth. (ఎనిమిదవ (enimidava).) Which vowel came off this time? (An i, not a u.) And how is the rule best held? (Drop whatever final vowel is there.)

segments.text: తొమ్మిదవ (tommidava) — "ninth".
తొమ్మిది becomes తొమ్మిదవ (tommidava). The doubled మ్మ in the middle is held, exactly as it is in the cardinal — the ending is added at the far end of the word and touches nothing on its way.
తొమ్మిదవ రోజు (tommidava rōju) — the ninth day.
Second i-ending in a row, and the same trade. One more and the ten are closed.

segments.text: పదవ (padava) — "tenth".
పది becomes పదవ (padava). Two syllables become three, and the trade is the same one you have now made nine times.
పదవ సంవత్సరం (padava saṁvatsaraṁ) — the tenth year.

That is the ten. Say them in order — modaṭi, reṇḍava, mūḍava, nālugava, aidava, ārava, ēḍava, enimidava, tommidava, padava — and count what you actually had to learn: one word and one ending. Latin needed ten separate words for the same stretch, and English still does.

blocks.title: Grammar Lens: every number you have, and every one you meet

segments.text: పదకొండవ (padakoṇḍava) — "eleventh".
పదకొండు becomes పదకొండవ (padakoṇḍava). Nothing new: the same final vowel goes, the same -వ arrives.
That is the point of this last lesson. The ending was never a fact about the numbers one to ten; it is a fact about numbers. Take any Telugu number you know and it works:
So there is no second list to learn above ten, and no list to learn below it either except the single word మొదటి. One irregular word, one ending, and every position on the number line is sayable.

segments.source: [PAUSE 1s]

segments.source: [YOU SAY: the swap on a bigger number — *padakoṇḍu* → *padakoṇḍava*]

segments.instruction: modaṭi is the only word; -va is the rest
segments.source: [YOU SAY: *modaṭi* is the only word; *-va* is the rest]
[PAUSE 3s]

segments.text: Say the eleventh. (పదకొండవ (padakoṇḍava).) How many separate ordinal words does Telugu have to be learned? (One — modaṭi.) And what makes all the others? (The number, minus its final vowel, plus -వ.)
